passages.title: Section II: Reading Comprehension Part A - Text 1
passages.content:
In the quest for the perfect lawn, homeowners across the country are replacing natural turf with artificial plastic grass. But the trend has spread to the highest gardening circles, with the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) banning fake grass from its prestigious shows because of the damage it causes to the environment.

The RHS says fake grass pollutes soils, harms wildlife and contributes to global warming. "Artificial grass harms biodiversity and damages our environment," says Mark Gush, head of environmental horticulture at the RHS. "It restricts the movement of worms, beetles and other soil life, and creates sterile green spaces that offer nothing to wildlife."

The RHS's decision comes as campaigners step up efforts to stop the spread of fake turf. Petitions calling for bans or taxes on plastic lawns have attracted tens of thousands of signatures, reflecting growing resistance among eco-conscious gardeners. They argue that at a time when nature is in crisis, covering gardens in plastic is disastrous for biodiversity.

However, suppliers and supporters of fake grass argue it has an important role to play. They point out that real lawns require vast quantities of water, mowing, weedkillers and fertilizers—all of which carry environmental impacts. Plastic lawns, by contrast, require no mowing or watering, making them ideal for urban areas with little time for maintenance. Furthermore, modern artificial turf can be recycled and does not necessarily exclude wildlife if surrounded by flowering borders and shrubs.

Government officials have largely stayed neutral in the debate. Ministers have declined to ban plastic grass outright or introduce special taxes, arguing that homeowners should be allowed to make their own choices.

However, environmental groups continue to urge the government to take stronger action, pointing out that existing regulations fall short of addressing plastic pollution in private spaces. For now, the battle between lovers of natural lawns and advocates of artificial turf remains one of the most controversial issues in modern gardening.

passages.title: Section II: Reading Comprehension Part A - Text 2
passages.content:
America's national parks are often hailed as the nation's "best idea," preserving millions of acres of wild landscapes and historic sites for public enjoyment. But beneath the majestic vistas, the national park system is grappling with an existential crisis: billions of dollars in deferred maintenance, deteriorating roads, crumbling visitor centers, and aging wastewater systems.

The National Park Service estimates its maintenance backlog at nearly $22 billion. Iconic sites like Yellowstone, Yosemite, and the Grand Canyon have faced catastrophic infrastructure failures, from burst sewer pipes to closed campgrounds. The crisis has been compounded by record crowds, as Americans flock to the outdoors in unprecedented numbers, straining resources and staff.

To bridge the funding gap, some policymakers and private contractors have advocated for increased commercialization and privatization of park services. Proposals include handing over campgrounds to private hospitality companies, introducing dynamic pricing, and allowing corporate sponsors to underwrite park facilities.

However, conservationists argue that privatization threatens the very spirit of the parks. Critics warn that private operators would prioritize profit over preservation, turning affordable, democratic public lands into exclusive resorts for wealthy tourists. Commercial development could degrade wildlife habitats and dilute the wilderness experience that draws visitors in the first place.

Public surveys reveal strong support for preserving the national parks without commercial compromise. In a recent economic survey of 700 taxpayers, an overwhelming majority expressed willingness to pay higher federal taxes to ensure parks are adequately funded and maintained by public agencies.

The national parks hold profound value not only as recreational retreats but as reservoirs of biodiversity and living monuments to American history. To safeguard this heritage, lawmakers must step up and provide reliable, permanent public funding rather than relying on piecemeal privatization schemes.

passages.title: Section II: Reading Comprehension Part A - Text 3
passages.content:
The Internet may be changing merely what we remember, not our capacity to do so, suggests Columbia University psychology professor Betsy Sparrow. In a groundbreaking series of experiments, Sparrow and her colleagues investigated how access to search engines affects human memory, demonstrating that people are becoming adept at remembering where to find information rather than memorizing the information itself.

This phenomenon, dubbed "cognitive offloading," allows our brains to delegate storage tasks to digital devices, freeing up mental bandwidth for other cognitive processes. Just as previous generations relied on books, rolodexes, and knowledgeable friends as external memory banks—a concept known as "transactive memory"—modern humans use the Internet as an omnipresent collective memory bank. Sparrow argues this adaptation does not indicate that our minds are declining, but rather that our cognitive habits are evolving to exploit powerful tools.

However, other cognitive scientists urge caution before declaring the digital shift entirely benign. Benjamin Storm, a memory researcher at the University of California, Santa Cruz, points out that while offloading mundane facts can be convenient, relying heavily on Google may weaken our ability to retain complex knowledge long enough to form deep connections and creative insights.

Furthermore, empirical studies on how internet use reshapes neural circuitry are still in their infancy. While early neuroimaging research shows that searching online stimulates brain activity in older adults, it remains too soon to know whether prolonged digital immersion fundamentally alters cognitive longevity.

Neither Sparrow nor Storm believes that the Internet is rotting our minds or permanently destroying our capacity to remember. Rather, they agree that our brains are remarkably plastic, continuously adapting their memory systems to mirror the informational ecosystem in which we live.

passages.title: Section II: Reading Comprehension Part A - Text 4
passages.content:
Parents of adolescents often describe the teenage years as an emotional roller coaster, a paradoxical period marked by bewildering contradictions. On the one hand, young people become fiercely independent, capable of extraordinary empathy, altruism, and deep peer loyalty. On the other hand, they can be moody, reckless, and alarmingly prone to impulsive risk-taking.

For decades, psychological literature focused predominantly on the dark side of adolescence, framing it as a phase of vulnerability and deficit. But a new wave of research led by Dutch developmental psychologist Eveline Crone offers a fresh, more nuanced perspective. Crone's work emphasizes that adolescence is not a neurological defect to be survived, but a critical evolutionary window of opportunity and social learning.

In an extensive study surveying over 200 youths aged 11 to 28, Crone and her team analyzed both prosocial behaviors—such as sharing, volunteering, and defending classmates—and rebellious behaviors like rule-breaking and sensation-seeking. Surprisingly, the data revealed a strong positive correlation between prosociality and rebelliousness. The very teenagers who engaged in daring adventures were often the same individuals who showed the greatest capacity for generosity and teamwork.

Crucially, the study showed that prosocial behavior follows the same developmental trajectory as risk-taking: both tend to peak during middle-to-late adolescence before plateauing in early adulthood.

What explains this intriguing dualism? Researchers point to "reward sensitivity." During adolescence, brain regions linked to social belonging and reward processing undergo rapid maturation, making teenagers hypersensitive to social recognition, praise, and peer approval. Seeking this social reward drives them to take bold chances—sometimes in reckless ways, but just as often in constructive, collaborative ways that prepare them for adulthood.

passages.title: Section II: Reading Comprehension Part B
passages.content:
Directions: Read the following text and match each of the persons in the left column (Questions 41-45) with their corresponding viewpoints listed in the right column (A-G).

Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (10 points)

Net-Zero Rules Set to Send Cost of New Homes and Extensions Soaring

[I] New building regulations aimed at improving energy efficiency are set to increase the price of new homes, as well as those of extensions and loft conversions on existing ones.

[II] The rules, which came into effect on Wednesday in England, are part of government plans to reduce the UK's carbon emissions to net zero by 2050. They set new standards for ventilation, energy efficiency and heating, and state that new residential buildings must have charging points for electric vehicles.

[III] The moves are the most significant change to building regulations in years, and industry experts say they will inevitably lead to higher prices at a time when a shortage of materials and high labour costs are already driving up bills.

[IV] Brian Berry, chief executive of the Federation of Master Builders, says the measures will require new materials, testing methods, products and systems to be installed. "All this comes at an increased cost during a time when prices are already sky high. Inevitably, consumers will have to pay more," he says.

[V] Gareth Belsham, of surveyors Naismiths, says people who are upgrading, or extending their home, will be directly affected. "The biggest changes relate to heating and insulation," he explains. "There are new rules concerning the amount of glazing used in extensions, and any new windows or doors must be highly insulated."

[VI] Windows and doors will have to adhere to higher standards, while there are new limits on the amount of glazing you can have to reduce unwanted heat from the sun.

[VII] Thomas Goodman, of MyJobQuote, says this will bring in new restrictions for extensions. "Glazing on windows, doors and roof lights must cover no more than 25% of the floor area to prevent heat loss," he says.

[VIII] As the rules came into effect last Wednesday, property developers were rushing to file plans just before the deadline. Any plans submitted before that date are considered to be under the previous rules, and can go ahead as long as work starts before 15 June next year.

[IX] Builders which have costed projects, but have not filed the paperwork, may need to go back and submit fresh estimates, says Marcus Jefford of Build Aviator.

[X] Materials prices are already up 25% in the last two years. How much overall prices will increase as a result of the rule changes is not clear. "Whilst admirable in their intentions, they will add to the cost of housebuilding at a time when many already feel that they are priced out of homeownership," says Jonathan Rolande of the National Association of Property Buyers. "An average extension will probably see around £3,000 additional cost thanks to the new regs."

[XI] John Kelly, a construction lawyer at Freeths law firm, believes prices will eventually come down. But not in the immediate future. "As the marketplace adapts to the new requirements, and the technologies that support them, the scaling up of these technologies will eventually bring costs down, but in the short term, we will all have to pay the price of the necessary transition," he says.

[XII] However, the long-term effects of the changes will be more comfortable and energy-efficient homes, adds Andrew Mellor, of PRP architects. "Homeowners will probably recoup that cost over time in energy bill savings. It will obviously be very volatile at the moment, but they will have that benefit over time."

is overpraised in the annual show

questions.stem: Sparrow's study shows that with the Internet, the human mind
questions.explanation: 【考点精析】事实细节题。首段及第二段 Sparrow 教授的实验证明互联网让人们善于记住何处能找到信息而非死记具体信息本身（remembering where to find information rather than memorizing the information itself），表明人类大脑改变了记忆关注的焦点，选 C。

frees up mental energy for thinking

questions.explanation: 【考点精析】观点推断题。第二段末尾 Sparrow 认为这种数字转向并不意味着思维退化，而是认知习惯为了利用强大工具所发生的演进（cognitive habits are evolving），支持互联网改变和重塑了我们的学习与获取知识的方式，选 A。
